problem: Existing space-grounding methods map spatial expressions to fixed coordinates or pixel maps and struggle with positional ambiguity, referential ambiguity (multiple identical objects) and composite instructions with many referring expressions.
motivation: Robots must localize places to reach or place objects from instructions like 'left of the box and close to the plate'. Such instructions are ambiguous and compositional, so a grounder should keep a probability distribution over locations and refine it as each new expression arrives.
key_idea: Ground space as a mixture of instance-wise polar distributions over scene-graph objects, predicted by a GPS-layer graph network that is updated incrementally for each relation tuple parsed by an LLM.
insight: Incremental updates with a scene-graph network (using semantic and geometric relations) keep accuracy high as the number of expressions grows, while baselines fail at four to six expressions. The LLM parser handles diverse phrasings where SREM's fixed parser fails, e.g. SREM scores 1.5 on ParaGon's compositional task and 42.5 on simple versus 90.5 and 80.0 for LINGO-Space. The polar distribution also represents 'far', which the baselines cannot. No formal component ablation is reported; the evidence comes from cross-benchmark comparisons.
method: Scene-graph generator: Grounding DINO boxes with CLIP image features as nodes (coordinate, box, visual feature) and CLIP-encoded spatial predicates (near, in) as directed edges.

LLM semantic parser: ChatGPT with a task description and 3 in-context demonstrations decomposes an instruction into action, source and target relation tuples (referenced object, predicate). These are embedded with the CLIP text encoder.

Polar-distribution mixture: each object j gets a weight w_j, a Gaussian over distance and a Von Mises over angle. Softplus enforces non-negativity, 1/kappa is predicted, and atan2 gives the mean angle.

Incremental estimation network: a stack of GPS layers (GINE MPNN plus Transformer global attention) takes coordinate positional encoding, visual, reference and predicate features, and the max-pooled previous model state. It outputs the distribution for each relation i conditioned on the previous one.
Loss: lambda*NLL of the ground-truth location under the mixture + (1-lambda)*cross-entropy on the mixture weights, applied sequentially for each relation.
Composite benchmark: a new task with 2-7 objects, semantically identical distractors, 10 directional predicates and 1-6 phrases at test, scored as #satisfied/|relations|.

setting.backbone: ChatGPT (frozen, parser) + CLIP encoders + GPS-layer graph network (GINE + Transformer, trained from scratch) + Grounding DINO detector
setting.training_data: Small per-task simulated tabletop datasets: 100 samples per task (400 scenes for ParaGon's benchmark, 200 for the composite task), tested on 200-300 samples; ChatGPT parser is prompted with 3 demonstrations
setting.observation: top-down RGB-D image (640x320) to scene graph; LiDAR-based bounding boxes on the real robot
setting.action_space: target location x in R^2 (2D placement or goal position), chosen as the argmax of the predicted distribution
setting.privileged: Assumes an optimal scene graph and ground-truth locations from bounding boxes; the scene-graph generator is assumed to produce an optimal graph

numbers.extra: trained on 200 samples without identical objects or repeated predicates

numbers_note: Not a navigation benchmark. Table 1 has 12 tasks; only representative rows are listed here. Other LINGO-Space results: close-seen 86.0, close-unseen 81.0, far-seen 95.5, far-unseen 95.0, comp-one-step-unseen 96.5.
results: LINGO-Space beats CLIPort, ParaGon and SREM on 11 of 12 single-expression tasks and on all four composite tasks. On composite tasks it is up to 62 points above the second-best method, and 22.6 above ParaGon's published 67.9 on the compositional task. On close/far predicates it wins on far but trails SREM on close (86.0 vs 91.0).
limitations: Assumes an optimal scene graph and known object positions, and is evaluated only with synthetic structured instructions in simulated 2D tabletop scenes.
Ignores object volume, which causes a small loss on behind-seen-colors; the closest baseline SREM beats it on 'close' tasks.
Real-world navigation is only a qualitative demonstration with no quantitative results.
